concept.name: Bear call spread
concept.definition: A bear call spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short call at a lower strike and a long call at a higher strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net credit. It profits if the underlying stays below the short strike, with fixed maximum gain (the credit) and maximum loss.
concept.intuition: You sell a call to bet the stock won't rise past your strike, and buy a higher call as a stop-loss so a rally can't hurt you beyond a known amount.
concept.mechanics: Net credit received at entry. Maximum gain = credit if the underlying finishes at or below the short strike; maximum loss = (strike width - credit) above the long strike. The CFTC describes the call bear spread as purchasing the higher-strike call and selling the lower-strike call.
concept.formula: Max gain = net credit; max loss = (K2 - K1) - net credit; breakeven = K1 + net credit, where K1 < K2 are the call strikes.
concept.failure_modes: Frequent small credits are punctuated by losses several times larger; assignment of the short leg near or after expiration can leave a residual stock position (pin risk). Selling calls into strong uptrends repeatedly loses.
concept.misconceptions: A high probability of keeping the credit is not the same as positive expectancy — the loss when wrong is a multiple of the credit. Credit received is not 'income'; it is payment for accepting bounded but real downside.
concept.example: Sell the XYZ $100 call for $4, buy the $105 call for $1.50: credit $2.50. If XYZ stays at or below $100, keep $250; above $105, lose $250.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
